episodes.176239: A storm system and its associated cold front racing across the Great Plains combined with moist southerly flow at the surface resulted in a line of thunderstorms that impacted Middle Tennessee on February 16, 2023. As this line moved into the area that provided abundant wind shear and sufficient instability, they strengthened and quickly turned severe. Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were received, and three tornadoes were confirmed across southern Middle Tennessee. While these three tornadoes were weak with 2 EF0s and 1 EF1, they were the first tornadoes in Middle Tennessee since January 1, 2022.
episodes.176244: Rainfall amounts of 2.5-4 fell over the course of a few hours on the evening of February 16th. Widespread flooding occurred across portions of Cullman, Marshall, and into portions of Jackson and Dekalb Counties. Parts of I-65 were shut down, and several water rescues occurred in Cullman County that evening thanks to thunderstorms repeatedly moving across these areas in a very warm and moist airmass for mid-February.
episodes.176404: Heavy rain was triggered by a cold front slowly displacing a warm sector whose precipitable water anomaly was near the maximum for the day.
episodes.176405: Heavy rain was triggered by a cold front slowly displacing a warm sector whose precipitable water anomaly was near the maximum for the day.
episodes.176461: Prolonged rainfall over a 24- to 25-hour period ended around 8 AM EST on February 17th, which resulted in localized minor river flooding across portions of southeast West Virginia (SEWV).  Unusual warmth during most of the river meant no frozen ground, snow cover or river ice in the area.  However, MRMS CREST indicated that the ground was still 50 to 75 percent saturated from widespread rainfall during the 12th and 13th, just a few days prior.  On the morning of the 16th, SEWV was located on the south side of a stationary front draped near the Ohio River.  Strong southwesterly windflow carried deep moisture from the Gulf of Mexico across the area, with precipitable water values (PWATs) in excess of 1.0 inch through much of the day on the 16th.  PWATs would increase to around 1.2 inches by sunrise of the 17th, just as a supporting upper level trough began to push across the Appalachian chain.  Rainfall rates were generally under a quarter inch per hour on the 16th, but began to increase during the overnight hours as the trough approached, in some instances exceeding an inch per hour for brief periods of time as a few thunderstorms developed, supported by Most-Unstable Layer CAPE values increasing to over 1,000 J/Kg ahead of the approaching trough.  Total rainfall amounts through the event ranged from 2.25 to locally 3.50 inches, resulting in minor river flooding along the Greenbrier, Bluestone and Meadow Rivers, as well as Anthony Creek.  Other smaller tributaries experienced minor flooding as well.  No flash flooding occurred.  Reported impacts were limited to flooded roads with little to no damage.
episodes.176462: Prolonged rainfall over a 24- to 25-hour period ended around 8 AM EST on February 17th, which resulted in localized minor river flooding across portions of western Virginia. Unusual warmth during most of the river meant no frozen ground, snow cover or river ice in the area. However, MRMS CREST indicated that the ground was still 50 to 75 percent saturated from widespread rainfall during the 12th and 13th, just a few days prior. On the morning of the 16th, western Virginia was located on the south side of a stationary front draped near the Ohio River. Strong southwesterly windflow carried deep moisture from the Gulf of Mexico across the area, with precipitable water values (PWATs) in excess of 1.0 inch through much of the day on the 16th. PWATs would increase to around 1.2 inches by sunrise of the 17th, just as a supporting upper level trough began to push across the Appalachian chain. Rainfall rates were generally under a quarter inch per hour on the 16th, but began to increase during the overnight hours as the trough approached, in some instances exceeding an inch per hour for brief periods of time as a few thunderstorms developed, supported by Most-Unstable Layer CAPE values increasing to over 1,000 J/Kg ahead of the approaching trough. Total rainfall amounts through the event ranged from 1.75 to locally 2.50 inches, resulting in minor river flooding along the Cowpasture, Bluestone and Clinch Rivers.  Other smaller tributaries experienced minor flooding as well.  Multiple other rivers and creeks rose to Action stage, but remained within their banks.  No flash flooding occurred.  Reported impacts were limited to flooded roads with little to no damage.
episodes.176590: A stationary front located near West Virginia on the morning of February 16th acted as a link between two low pressure systems streaming north and south of the area. Early morning thunderstorms promoted locally heavy rain, with a second round taking place later that evening as the front made eastward progress. ||Prolonged periods of rain led to flooding across the central and southern portions of the state. Most notable impacts from flooding occurred in Milton, where over one hundred homes observed basement flooding and high water surrounding the neighborhood. One to three inches of rain fell during this time, maintaining saturated conditions and flooding concerns on February 17th and into the next day before the floodwaters began to recede.||In Fayette County, an infant passed away due to a car being swept away from fast moving water near Paint Creek.||Several rivers rose above their banks in the midst of the event, including parts of the Mud River, Coal River, and Guyandotte River.
episodes.176597: Portions of southeast Ohio observed flooding beginning on the afternoon of February 16th in response to heavy rainfall ahead of a cold frontal passage. Rain began early in the morning with scattered thunderstorms, and picked up intensity by the afternoon and evening as the front pressed closer into the area. Saturated soils gradually resulted in high water concerns along roadways in Lawrence, Athens, and Gallia Counties through the evening of the 16th. Symmes Creek rose out of its banks during the predawn hours on the 17th, returning below bankfull level just before midnight.
episodes.176598: Rain and thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of February 16th ahead of a low pressure system and surface cold front. Earlier that morning, a round of thunderstorms swept through eastern Kentucky, priming the area for potential flooding concerns as heavier rain was anticipated heading into the afternoon. By the evening hours, over one to two inches of rain had fallen, contributing to flooding in Greenup County and prolonged flooding around the town of Cannonsburg in Boyd County. Multiple road closures were observed through much of the next day until floodwaters finally receded.
episodes.176599: Periods of heavy rainfall resulted from a progressing low pressure system and surface cold front late on February 16th into the 17th. As rain continued across southwest Virginia on the morning of the 17th, minor flooding was observed along local roads in Buchanan County into the afternoon hours. A strong thunderstorm passing through the area early that morning also resulted in a tree to be blown down in the town of Pearly.||Runoff from the excessive rainfall spilled into Cranes Nest River and Pound River during the overnight hours between February 16th and 17th, resulting in the rivers to rise out of their banks. Both of the river gages at these points observed the rivers cresting on the morning of the 17th and then finally returning to their banks a few hours later by the early afternoon.
episodes.176905: Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall, falling at rates of one to three inches per hour, generated flashing flooding which forced road closures for parts of Big island's Kau and Puna Districts.
episodes.177028: Widespread rain with numerous embedded thunderstorms persisted through the overnight hours of the 15th into the early morning hours of the 16th. Locally heavy rainfall caused some pockets of flash flooding of roads and low spots. A surface low pressure system moved northeast across Arkansas along a warm front that extended northeast through the lower Ohio Valley. Rainfall became widespread along the warm front as the low pressure center approached the Ohio Valley.
episodes.178075: Scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms associated with a cold front produced gusty winds across portions of the York River.
episodes.178090: A low pressure center was slowly tracking into western Kentucky during the first part of the day on Wedensday, with a stationary front positioned along the Ohio River, and keeping much of eastern Kentucky in a warm, moist, and unstable airmass. Showers and thunderstorms were ongoing through much of the morning, leading to multiple flooding reports across the region. Then by the afternoon, the low pressure center had moved into Indiana, allowing the stationary front to lift north as a warm front, and a cold front to begin traversing the western half of the state. A more progressive line of strong showers and thunderstorms moved through eastern Kentucky ahead of this cold front, finally coming to an end after the cold front had passed through overnight. Multiple reports of downed trees and additional flooding were reported as heavy rain and strong winds complimented some of these storms.
episodes.178254: A line of thunderstorms moved into north and central Georgia during the early morning hours of February 17, 2023. This line of storms produced isolated wind damage and with a highly sheared environment, allowed for a tornado to spin up just on the outskirts of LaGrange.

events.narrative: A NWS employee came upon a road block around 5762 KY-15, northwest of Bethany, due to a hillside/driveway being washed out onto the road and making the road impassable.
Severe thunderstorm winds downed a tree along Monterey Highway near Yankeetown Church in Sparta. Damages are estimated.
Quarter size hail was reported near Bon Air.
Severe thunderstorm winds downed trees along Mack Floyd Road near Sparta. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rain across Lawrence County flooded nearly all low water crossings and forced their closure. Any damages are not known.
Big Lost Creek Road near Shaws Bridge Road was blocked due to flooding. Three Prong Road was underwater for a brief period of time due to Three Prong Branch rising out of its banks.
Heavy rain across Marshall County flooded and closed several roads in the county. Any damages are not known.
Flash flooding along Hogjaw Road near Arab. Water covering the road, rising up to vehicle doors in some areas.

Pictures and videos on social media show a large SUV having been swept into a water-filled ditch in front of River Bend Apartments in Salyersville, after trying to drive through the flooded roadway (KY-7/Gardner Trail) and losing traction. The car was mostly submerged in the water, but all occupants were able to escape the flooded vehicle.
Water covering several roadways and ditches overflowing in and around Downtown Arab.

Continuous rounds of rain led to prolonged flooding around the Pax area. High water was first observed on the evening of February 16th along Packs Branch Road and portions of Paint Creek Road. The next morning, Paint Creek remained out of its banks and continued to spill onto Paint Creek Road. A vehicle drove into the flooded road and was swept away along with an infant. Local authorities later found the infant had drowned.
Deep moving water reported over the roadway on the 2300 Block of County Road 47.
Both North and Southbound lanes of I-65 shut down near MM 308 due to flash flooding. About a foot of water over the roadway. Numerous other roads are flooded in Cullman County.

Roads in and around Chapmanville observed high water late in the evening of February 16th as adjacent creeks rose above their banks. These included Perry Branch Road, Browns Run Road, and Garrett Fork Road.
Several roads across the county were flooded.
Several roadways were flooded across the county.
Several roadways were flooded across the county.
A mudslide due to heavy rainfall was reported along Tiprell Road on a broadcast media article online. Event time estimated.
Heavy rain across White County flooded several roads, rendering them impassable. Any damages are not known.

Shortly after midnight on February 17th, the Cranes Nest River in Clintwood rose above its 11 foot bankfull level. The river remained its banks through the late morning hours that day, cresting at 12.09 feet in the process. This resulted in minor flooding along low spots on Cranes Nest River Camp road leading up to the campground.

The Mud River and other smaller creeks within the town of Milton rose out of their banks and resulted in an inundation of water into residential homes and businesses within the community. The river crested at 27 feet on the afternoon of February 17th, which was the main culprit behind the major flooding around the town. Over a hundred homes were affected by high water, with a dozen observing flooding damage and many roads were closed due to the high water concerns. The floodwaters receded and the river returned to its banks early in the afternoon on the 18th.
Multiple roads continued to be flooded around the southeastern half of the county.
A tree was blown down near Route 604 in Pearly.

The Pound River in Norland rose above its 8 foot bankfull level around dawn on the morning of February 17th. The river crested just below 9 feet a few hours later and returned to its banks the same afternoon. While the river was out of its banks, several sections of Camp Creek Road around the community were under water.

The tornado began northeast of the airport near the intersection of Gordon Road and Swanson Dr. Sporadic EF-0 tree damage occurred as it traveled east before intensifying to a low end EF-1 near Callaway Stadium on the LaGrange College campus. Roof damage occurred both to a local brewery and Georgia health department building. The most considerable damage occurred to a house near this location along Forrest Avenue where a large oak tree was uprooted and fell into the home. Several bleachers were tossed into a brick and metal fence destroying a portion of the fence. Damage continued to the northeast where numerous trees were uprooted and several homes sustained minor roof damage. Another area of EF-1 damage was observed at the George F. Harris Baseball Complex where a few trees were uprooted and several were snapped. The tornado then entered another area of homes where some tree damage and uprooted trees were noted before entering a shopping district along Highway 109 just west of I-85. Several businesses had damaged signs and minor roof damage. A local gas station had windows blown out of a car wash. Some additional damage continued to the northeast with some trees downed before the tornado lifted near the intersection of I-85 and Highway 109.
KATL ASOS reported wind gust of 71mph as line of thunderstorms pushed through the area.
Several roads were closed across the county due to flooding during the early morning.

The tunnel under the railroad tracks on Old Bramwell Road was flooded.  One car became stranded in the floodwater trying to drive through the tunnel. Water eventually rose up to the hood of the car.  Flooding was most likely caused due to poor drainage within the tunnel.  The nearby Bluestone River was several feet below flood stage at the onset of flooding within the tunnel.  A nearby personal weather station indicated that rainfall rates since midnight on the 17th never exceeded 0.5 inch per hour with a storm total amount of 1.7 inches, not an unusual event.  The damage estimate is for flooding to the car.
Portions of Germany Road were closed due to heavy runoff from prolonged rainfall.  No damage to the road was reported.

The Cooperative Weather Observer at Burkes Garden reported multiple streams out of their banks during the morning of February 17th due to prolonged rainfall during the 24 hours prior.  Some of the streams were observed flowing across local roads and bridges a few inches deep.  No damage was reported and the streams receded back within their banks by late morning after rainfall ended.
Multiple roads within Abingdon were closed as pictured on social media.

Symmes Creek in the town of Aid rose above its 19 foot bankfull level near sunrise on the morning of February 16th. The creek rose to 19.87 feet twenty-four hours later before returning to its banks during the early morning hours of February 18th. This prolonged period of time being out of its banks caused minor flooding issues along State Routes 217 and 378 in and around Aid.

A National Weather Service employee reported signs that Anthony Creek, as well as multiple tributaries of the creek were out of their banks and covering Highway 92 near the community of Neola, WV during the 17th.  No damage was reported, though removal of debris was likely necessary.
Lick Creek rose out of its banks in Danville and spilled onto Lick Creek Road.

The James River and Kanawha Turnpike was closed due to flooding of small creeks between the communities of Rainelle and Meadow Bluff.  The road was reopened after flooding receded, with no damage reported.

In the town of Bradshaw, the Tug Fork rose above its 10 foot bankfull level on the morning of February 17th. The river returned to its banks later that evening, cresting at 12.31 feet around midday. While the Tug Fork was out of its banks, minor flooding was observed near homes residing along the river.

Brad Paisley community park was flooded up to the foundation of a pavilion there from water rising out of Wades Creek.  The park is located at the confluence of Wades Creek and Howard Creek.  No damage to the park was reported.

On the morning of February 17th, Knapp Creek in Huntersville rose above its 9 foot bankfull level. The creek crested at 9.83 feet, which resulted in minor flooding along Browns Creek Road and the fields adjacent to the creek. By later on that afternoon, the creek returned to its banks.

The stream gage at Anthony Creek near Anthony (ANYW2) crested at 15.87 feet (7,865 cfs) at 1:20 pm EST on 2/17/23.  This is roughly a 2-year event (50% AEP) per USGS Streamstats for this location and the highest crest on record since 2014.  The Anthony Creek basin received between 1.75 and 2.5 inches of rainfall in about a 24-hour period ending 8:00 AM EST on 2/17/23, falling over ground that was moistened by widespread rainfall on the 12th and 13th a few days prior.  There was no snow cover prior to this event.
The South Fork Powell River inundated Proctor Street on both sides of the bridge that crosses the river near Wallens Ridge Blvd.
Flooding was observed along Front Street in Spencer.
Local roads in and around Vansant observed high water issues for a period of time.
A few roads in the county were closed for a period of time due to high water issues from flooding. These included Coal River Road in Glen Daniel and Mattsville Road in the town of Stover.

The Clinch River at Richlands, VA (RLRV2) crested at 11.22 feet (Flood stage is 10 feet).  This was caused by between 1.75 and 2.75 inches of rain over a 24-25 hour period. No snow melt or frozen ground was involved, but the ground was moist from widespread rainfall on the 12th and 13th a few days prior.  This caused flooding of several streets in town that typically flood when the river exceeds 10 feet, including along 4th Street, Britts Park Road and Alleghany Avenue near the Richlands Police Station.  Further west, Clinch River Road and Matney Lane were also flooded and impassible.  At least three automobiles were known to be flooded deep enough where water entered the passenger compartment.

The Big Coal River in Ashford rose above its 17 foot bankfull level on the morning of February 17th. The river crested at 17.43 feet a few days later in the early afternoon of February 19th before returning to its banks that evening. In the midst of the river being out of its banks, minor flooding was observed along Ridgeview Nellis Road just before the Ashford Nellis Road bridge.
Several roads in the Lynco community was impassable for a period of time due to flooding. In the town Clear Fork, Route 971 near Westside High School was also closed due to high water issues.
Several roads in the southeastern portions of Buchanan County were closed for a period of time due to flooding. These included Route 622, Route 600, and Route 657 near the town of Davenport.

Properties and vehicles flooded near the intersection of Hwy 58 and Route 706 near Tacoma. Most of the homes in the area were mobile homes whose elevated living spaces seemed to remain above the flood waters that inundated the ground beneath them. Captured by drone video displayed on social media.
Between the towns of Smithers and Boomer, Route 60 was closed due to flooding from the Kanawha River.
Portions of Highway 43 were reported to have standing water on them up to a foot deep.  The road was closed briefly to allow the water to run off.  No damage was reported.

The Clear Fork along the Guyandotte River rose above its 11 foot bankfull level on the morning of February 17th, cresting at 11.09 feet early in the afternoon, and then returned to its banks later that evening. While the river was out of its banks, sections of Charlie Hatfield Road/County Route 6 were flooded.

A single vehicle attempted to cross a flooded roadway near Wood Valley Road. The vehicle was carried downstream with operator inside. When emergency personnel arrived, the operator had already self-extricated from the vehicle.

Multiple roads were closed as a result of the repeated rounds of heavy rainfall, including Highway 11 at Kawa Flats, Wood Valley Road, Pohaku Drive, East Kawailani Street, and Kaalaiki Road. Railroad Ave. was also closed in both directions from East Lanikaula St. to Kukil St. Additionally, Piake St. and Llima St. were affected by water flooding the bridge at Paauau Gulch near Pahala.

The gage along the Coal River in Tornado observed a rise above the river's 25 foot flood stage on the afternoon of February 17th. The river crested at 25.31 feet that evening and returned to its banks just after midnight on the 18th. While in flood, the river caused portions of Smith Creek Road to close due to the high water concerns. Other sections of Coal River Road upstream from the Tornado bridge were also flooded.
The Greenbrier River at Alderson, WV crested at 14.69 feet (flood stage is 14 feet). This flooding is between a 2- and a 5-year average recurrence interval for this location.
Wind gust of 39 knots was measured at Yorktown USCG Station.

The Tug Fork in Williamson rose above its 27 foot flood stage late in the afternoon on February 17th. The river crested at 28.7 feet later that evening and returned to its banks a few hours after midnight on the 18th. While above its flood stage, backwater from the Tug Fork spilled onto Route 612 in South Williamson and caused minor traffic obstructions. The water treatment plant in Williamson closed its flood gate to help prevent water from the river to spill into the area until the floodwaters receded.

The Cowpasture River near Clifton Forge, VA crested at 10.40 feet (Flood stage is 10 feet).  This was a little over a 2-year event (50% AEP) per USGS Streamstats. The flooding was caused by between 1.5 and 2.75 inches of rain over a 24-25 hour period. No snow melt or frozen ground was involved, but the ground was moist from widespread rainfall on the 12th and 13th a few days prior.  Minor lowland flooding was the only impact observed.
The Green River rose above flood stage for a few days. There was minor flooding of low-lying woods and fields near the river.
